summary:
Our project is an immersive, interactive simulation that introduces users to the complexities of NASA mission design. Unlike many traditional educational projects, our web application goes beyond simply explaining space exploration; it allows users to experience the engineering, scientific research, and decision-making involved in planning real space missions. Users can design spacecraft, select scientific instruments, calculate trajectories and orbits using physics-based formulas and NASA’s General Mission Analysis Tool (GMAT), and explore planetary environments using scientific data. 
To make these complex concepts accessible and engaging, we incorporate interactive controls, customizable spacecraft, and cinematic 3D cutscenes developed with Three.js. The application also provides clear, contextual explanations that help users understand unfamiliar concepts, recognize mistakes, and learn from their decisions rather than simply telling them whether they are right or wrong. 
This project is important because it makes the science and engineering behind space exploration more accessible to students and aspiring scientists. By allowing users to experiment with mission design and experience the consequences of their choices, we aim to transform abstract STEM concepts into practical, engaging experiences. Ultimately, we hope to inspire curiosity about aerospace engineering while giving users a deeper understanding of the work required to make space missions possible.
details:
The application is organized around a series of interconnected mission stages, each presenting a different engineering challenge. Users must make decisions using the information available to them, while the simulation tracks how those decisions affect the spacecraft and its mission. 

One important feature is the spacecraft construction system. Users can choose between different components and instruments, each with its own advantages and disadvantages. These selections influence the spacecraft's overall mass, power requirements, scientific capabilities, and reliability. This creates realistic engineering trade-offs, where adding more equipment does not necessarily produce a better mission. The simulation also includes interactive instrument panels. Rather than receiving automatic results, users must operate equipment, interpret measurements, and determine how to respond. Unexpected events, such as equipment malfunctions, radiation exposure, and resource shortages, introduce additional challenges that require users to adapt their plans. For planetary surface exploration, we developed a rover system with movement controls, a minimap, randomly generated geological formations, and scientific instruments. Users can navigate the terrain, investigate rock formations, conduct scans, and collect samples. The rover also has limited resources, requiring users to consider battery consumption and the distance needed to return safely. 

We also incorporate a competitive multiplayer mode in which players race against one another to complete space missions. Players must design their spacecraft, make engineering decisions, manage resources, and overcome mission challenges while competing to achieve their objectives before their opponents. Success depends not only on speed but also on effective planning, efficient resource management, and sound engineering decisions. This adds replayability and a competitive element to the simulation while allowing players to test their mission-design strategies against others.

We placed particular emphasis on making the interface approachable. Contextual guides explain individual instruments, controls, and scientific concepts through short explanations rather than overwhelming users with large amounts of text. We also incorporated visual representations of mathematical equations to help users understand how changing variables affects mission calculations. Three.js powers the interactive 3D models, environments, and cutscenes, while mathematical calculations in Javascript handle mission parameters such as orbital mechanics and spacecraft trajectories. We also use NASA's General Mission Analysis Tool (GMAT) and NASA scientific datasets to connect the simulation to established aerospace engineering methods and real planetary observations.

Throughout development, we have focused on combining scientific accuracy with an accessible interface. Our goal is to create a simulation in which users can experiment with increasingly complex engineering problems while seeing how individual decisions influence an entire space mission.
